> AGENT

Confirmed at the source. go-git v6's `plumbing/transport/serve.go:45`:

```go
if forPush {
    // TODO: support thin-pack
    _ = ar.Capabilities.Set(capability.NoThin)
    ...
}
```

So **go-git's receive-pack unconditionally advertises `no-thin`** because its server-side pack processing doesn't support thin-pack reference resolution yet (it's a `TODO`). `entire-server` uses go-git's transport for its HTTPS smart-HTTP endpoint, so it inherits this limitation.

This is why `sync` works against entire and `replicate` doesn't — `sync` falls back to the materialized strategy which encodes a complete pack, but `replicate` is relay-only by design and needs the target to accept thin packs.

## What this means for testing

Your local `entire` target genuinely **cannot be a replicate target today**, until go-git's receive-pack grows thin-pack support. Options in decreasing order of effort:

**A. Test replicate against something other than entire.** Any real git host supports thin packs: Gitea (in Docker), Gogs, a throwaway GitHub repo, GitLab, a local `git daemon` with proper git-core, etc. Quickest path:

```bash
# Gitea in 30 seconds
docker run -d --name gitea -p 3000:3000 -v /tmp/gitea:/data gitea/gitea:latest
# Create user + empty repo via http://localhost:3000, then:
TGT=http://localhost:3000/<user>/<repo>.git
go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate --stats --json $SRC $TGT | jq .
```

**B. Fix go-git's receive-pack to process thin packs.** The `TODO: support thin-pack` comment says exactly what's missing. That's a meaningful undertaking — the server needs to resolve delta-from references against the repo's object store before or during pack ingestion. Worth doing, not a one-afternoon job.

**C. Change replicate to accept no-thin targets by requesting a non-thin pack from source.** You can ask an upload-pack server for a non-thin pack by *not* setting `thin-pack` in the fetch capabilities (or by setting `no-thin` explicitly in some variants). The source would then send a fully self-contained pack. This keeps replicate relay-only but makes it a bit less efficient. If you want, I can prototype this — it'd be a small change: when target advertises `no-thin`, omit/negate the thin request on the source side so the relayed pack works.

Option C might be the right move — it preserves replicate's "no materialization" guarantee while widening compatibility. Worth discussing before coding.

> AGENT

Good — go-git's upload-pack also has `TODO: Support thin-pack`, and more importantly, **our `FetchPack` doesn't request the `thin-pack` capability anywhere**. By protocol rules, a source only emits thin packs when the client explicitly asks for them. So we're *already* fetching non-thin packs — the `SupportsReplicateRelay` rejection is over-cautious for replicate's actual behavior.

So the fix is simpler than I'd first suggested: just drop the rejection. No new flag needed, no protocol changes, no risk of accidentally pushing a thin pack to a no-thin target (source won't make one).

Let me implement and flip the tests:

  "new_string": "// SupportsReplicateRelay checks target-side capabilities required by\n// replication mode before looking at planned ref actions.\n//\n// Replicate tolerates targets that advertise \"no-thin\" because our\n// upload-pack client (gitproto.FetchPack) never requests the \"thin-pack\"\n// capability, so the source never emits a thin pack. The relayed pack is\n// always self-contained and safe to push to a no-thin receive-pack.\n// If gitproto.FetchPack ever begins requesting thin-pack, this check must\n// gain a matching fallback (omit the request, or explicitly advertise\n// NoThin on the source request) when target.NoThin is set.\nfunc SupportsReplicateRelay(target RelayTargetPolicy) (bool, string) {\n\tif !target.CapabilitiesKnown {\n\t\treturn false, \"replicate-missing-target-capabilities\"\n\t}\n\tif target.NoThin {\n\t\treturn true, \"replicate-target-capable-no-thin\"\n\t}\n\treturn true, \"replicate-target-capable\"\n}"
}

Committed as `1a477f8`. Now you should be able to replicate against your local `entire` target:

```bash
export SRC=https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes.git
export TGT=https://localhost:8080/git/test/git-sync-smoke-10

go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --stats --measure-memory --json \
  $SRC $TGT | jq '{operation_mode, relay, relay_reason, pushed, deleted, blocked}'
```

The JSON will show `relay_reason` including `replicate-target-capable-no-thin` when the target advertises no-thin, which is a useful observability signal if you ever need to debug pack size or transfer behavior.

One thing to watch: because the relayed pack is always full (not thin), overwrite/rewind scenarios against entire will transfer more bytes than they would against a thin-pack-capable target. For kubernetes/linux sized repos on incremental runs, the difference can be noticeable but is still bounded by the objects reachable from the refs being pushed. Not a correctness issue, just an efficiency footnote if you're benchmarking.

That worked end-to-end against your local `entire` target. 61 refs pushed through the bootstrap-relay path, no blocks, no errors — the full chain (keychain auth → entiredb lookup → HTTPS → no-thin-tolerant replicate → receive-pack) is functional.

A couple of follow-ups to squeeze more out of this smoke test:

**1. Re-run to exercise the no-op fast path:**

```bash
go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --stats --measure-memory --json \
  $SRC $TGT | jq '{operation_mode, pushed, skipped, relay_reason}'
```

Expect `pushed: 0`, `skipped: 61`, no receive-pack POST.

**2. Exercise the actual overwrite path** — rewind a branch on the target (or on the source) so a replicate run has to retarget:

```bash
# Find any ref + its parent commit from the source
BRANCH=$(curl -sk "$SRC/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack" | strings | grep -oE 'refs/heads/[^ ]+' | grep -v HEAD | head -1)

# Or just reset one target ref back a commit using git directly (easier than curl).
# Then re-run replicate and check for pushed>0 with non-bootstrap relay_reason.

> AGENT

That error doesn't have the `replicate relay failed: ... use sync instead` wrapping, which means it's from the **bootstrap-relay** path — same place the first run (the one that succeeded with 61 pushed) came from.

That strongly suggests replicate is still treating the target as empty. So either:

1. The first run didn't actually persist those 61 refs on the target, or
2. The second run isn't seeing them in the advertisement (different endpoint, different auth context, different user scope, etc.)

Quickest way to find out which is which:

```bash
# Verify target state directly
go run ./cmd/git-sync probe --json \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  $SRC $TGT | jq '{target_ref_count: (.target.refs | length), target_head: .target.refs["refs/heads/master"] // .target.refs["refs/heads/main"]}'
```

Also note — your last command dropped `--target-insecure-skip-tls-verify`. If that flag propagates (or doesn't) differently to auth vs. transport code, or if it affects whether `entiredb` refresh works, the token context may be different between runs. Put the flag back:

```bash
go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT | jq .
```

and see if the second run now no-ops as expected.

## About the `short pkt-line 4` error itself

That's `pktline.Read` failing because `io.ReadFull` got fewer than 4 bytes when reading the pktline length prefix — i.e., the receive-pack response body is effectively empty. Either:

- Target returned HTTP 200 with an empty body (server-side bug, connection cut, or truncation), or
- Sideband demuxer consumed everything as progress/error frames and left nothing for `ReportStatus.Decode`.

To isolate, capture the raw response next time it happens:

```bash
# Re-run with verbose once we have tls-skip back in:
go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate -v \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT 2>&1 | tee /tmp/replicate.log | tail -40
```

Verbose prints sideband progress, which often includes the server-side error message before the truncation.

My bet is on `--target-insecure-skip-tls-verify` being the difference. Entire likely serves a self-signed cert; without the flag the second connection may establish far enough to send but then abort before the response body is fully written, leaving you with an empty receive-pack response.

Ah, that reframes it — you're hitting a push-side failure on a very large bootstrap. "short pkt-line 4" means the receive-pack response body was empty (fewer than 4 bytes read for the pktline length prefix). Almost certainly the target closed the connection before replying, which happens on big pushes when the server has:

- a body size limit,
- a request timeout,
- an OOM during pack processing, or
- an upstream proxy buffering then dropping.

> AGENT

Confirmed — `--batch-max-pack-bytes` is only wired to the `bootstrap` subcommand, not `replicate`. Replicate's bootstrap fallback **does** honor `Config.BatchMaxPackBytes` internally (`internal/syncer/syncer.go:758`), but there's no CLI flag to set it on `replicate`.

## Immediate workaround: use `bootstrap` for the initial seed

For a repo this big, do a batched bootstrap first, then use `replicate` for incremental updates going forward:

```bash
# 256 MB batches — gets under most server body limits.
# Adjust --max-pack-bytes up if the source's single pack > 1 GB.
time go run ./cmd/git-sync bootstrap \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --batch-max-pack-bytes 268435456 \
  --max-pack-bytes 10737418240 \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT | tee /tmp/linux-bootstrap.json | jq '{pushed, batch_count, planned_batch_count, relay_reason}'

# From now on, incremental overwrites against the already-seeded target:
go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT | jq .
```

## Server-side diagnostic

Before (or while) you retry, watch the server log. `entire-server` sits behind connect-go (I saw those symbols in the binary earlier) which has body-size limits on gRPC. For a linux-sized push the culprit is almost certainly one of:

- connect-go message size limit — default 4 MiB for replies, often higher for requests but still bounded
- HTTP idle/read timeout
- OOM on the Raft-backed storage layer ingesting a 5 GB pack in one shot

```bash
grep -iE 'too large|exceeds|timeout|oom|kill|reset|cancel|abort' entire.log | tail -30
```

## Proper fix: add `--batch-max-pack-bytes` to `replicate` (and `sync`)

Would you like me to wire this flag through? Small change — the config plumbing already works, it's just the flag registration on `runSyncLike` that's missing. That way bootstrap-fallback inside replicate can batch without needing the user to drop down to the `bootstrap` subcommand.

> AGENT

The log doesn't tell us much — it only shows the restart at 16:53:45 followed by a clean Ctrl-C shutdown at 16:54:18, with **zero** entries for receive-pack/push/pack. So one of:

1. The log rolled or this is a fresh session *after* your failed linux run, so we're not seeing that run's server-side activity.
2. The server was brought down mid-push (I see `Ctrl-C pressed` in the shutdown tail) — which would exactly produce "short pkt-line 4" on the client because the connection dies before receive-pack writes its report-status.

Either way, for a push this size, batching is almost certainly needed. Let me wire `--batch-max-pack-bytes` into `replicate` and `sync` so replicate's bootstrap fallback can split the push:

> TOOL

> AGENT

Committed as `6a219a1`. Now retry the linux push with batching:

```bash
# Restart your entire dev env first if it's still down
cd ../../devenv && mise run dev &

# Back to git-sync, retry with batching. Adjust sizes to taste.
# 256 MiB per batch is usually a safe starting point:
export SRC=https://github.com/torvalds/linux.git
# (new empty target)

time go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --batch-max-pack-bytes 268435456 \
  --max-pack-bytes 10737418240 \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT 2>&1 | tee /tmp/linux-replicate.log | jq '{pushed, batching, batch_count, planned_batch_count, relay_reason, peak: .measurement.peak_heap_inuse_bytes}'
```

And tail `entire.log` in another terminal so we can catch any server-side error *while* the push runs. If it still hits "short pkt-line 4", the server log will almost certainly show the root cause this time (body size limit, OOM, timeout, raft commit failure).

## Knobs to tune if 256 MiB batches are still too large

```bash
--batch-max-pack-bytes 67108864    # 64 MiB
--batch-max-pack-bytes 16777216    # 16 MiB
```

Smaller batches = more receive-pack POSTs = higher total time but lower peak memory and fewer opportunities to hit a limit.

> AGENT

Short answer: with `-v` there's *some* progress (discrete milestone logs), but the server's sideband progress messages — the `Counting objects / Resolving deltas` lines git shows — are currently discarded. That's why a multi-minute push looks frozen.

## What you get today

With `-v`, `bootstrap.Execute` logs at milestone boundaries to stderr:

```
msg="bootstrap fetching refs from source" ref_count=...
msg="bootstrap pushing refs to target" ref_count=...
msg="bootstrap batch push checkpoint" ...
msg="bootstrap batch checkpoint complete" ...
msg="bootstrap batch branch finalized" branch=refs/heads/master
```

So you'll see a line when a batch starts, when it finishes, etc. — but nothing during the actual upload of each pack, and nothing about what the server is doing while it processes the batch.

## What's missing, and why

Two deliberate silencings in the code:

1. **`internal/gitproto/push.go:sendReceivePack`** demuxes sideband but passes `nil` for the progress sink — any "Counting / Compressing / Resolving" lines the server emits on channel 2 go to `/dev/null`.
2. **`buildV1UploadPackBody` / `fetchPackV2`** unconditionally send `no-progress` to the source, telling the source's upload-pack not to bother emitting progress at all.

Neither is conditional on `-v`. So even with verbose, you get no continuous feedback.

## Want me to wire it up?

Minimal change, ~15 lines:

- When `Verbose=true`, stop sending `no-progress` on upload-pack so the source emits progress.
- Route the fetch-side sideband progress channel and the push-side sideband progress channel to `os.Stderr`, prefixed with `source: ` / `target: ` so you can tell them apart.
- Default (non-verbose) stays quiet for scripted/JSON use.

That would give you a live stream during your linux push, something like:

```
source: Counting objects: 10000000, done.
source: Compressing objects: 37% (3712000/10000000)
source: Compressing objects: 100% (10000000/10000000), done.
target: Unpacking objects:  12% (1200000/10000000)
target: Resolving deltas:   58% (5800000/10000000)
```

Worth it? It's genuinely useful for anything over ~30s, and I can keep it behind `-v` so JSON/scripted callers are unaffected.

54	// buildUpdateRequest builds the receive-pack update request.
55	func buildUpdateRequest(
56		adv *packp.AdvRefs,
57		commands []PushCommand,
58		verbose bool,
59	) (*packp.UpdateRequests, bool, bool, error) {
60		req := packp.NewUpdateRequests()
61		if sb := PreferredSideband(adv.Capabilities); sb != "" {
62			_ = req.Capabilities.Set(sb)
63		}
64		if adv.Capabilities.Supports(capability.ReportStatus) {
65			_ = req.Capabilities.Set(capability.ReportStatus)
66		}
67	
68		hasDelete := false
69		hasUpdates := false
70		for _, cmd := range commands {
71			c := &packp.Command{Name: cmd.Name, Old: cmd.Old}
72			if cmd.Delete {
73				c.New = plumbing.ZeroHash
74				hasDelete = true
75			} else {
76				c.New = cmd.New
77				hasUpdates = true
78			}
79			req.Commands = append(req.Commands, c)
80		}
81	
82		if hasDelete {
83			if !adv.Capabilities.Supports(capability.DeleteRefs) {
84				return nil, false, false, fmt.Errorf("target does not support delete-refs")
85			}
86			_ = req.Capabilities.Set(capability.DeleteRefs)
87		}
88	
89		_ = verbose // progress handling is server-side in HTTP mode
90		return req, hasDelete, hasUpdates, nil
91	}

93	// sendReceivePack encodes and POSTs a receive-pack request, then decodes the report.
94	func sendReceivePack(
95		ctx context.Context,
96		conn *Conn,
97		req *packp.UpdateRequests,
98		packData io.Reader,
99	) error {
100		var header bytes.Buffer
101		if err := req.Encode(&header); err != nil {
102			return fmt.Errorf("encode update-request: %w", err)
103		}
104		body := io.Reader(bytes.NewReader(header.Bytes()))
105		if packData != nil {
106			body = io.MultiReader(body, packData)
107		}
108		reader, err := PostRPCStreamBody(ctx, conn, transport.ReceivePackService, body, false, "receive-pack push")
109		if err != nil {
110			return fmt.Errorf("target receive-pack: %w", err)
111		}
112		defer reader.Close()
113	
114		// Unwrap sideband if negotiated.
115		var respReader io.Reader = reader
116		if req.Capabilities.Supports(capability.Sideband64k) {
117			respReader = sideband.NewDemuxer(sideband.Sideband64k, reader)
118		} else if req.Capabilities.Supports(capability.Sideband) {
119			respReader = sideband.NewDemuxer(sideband.Sideband, reader)
120		}
121	
122		if req.Capabilities.Supports(capability.ReportStatus) {
123			report := packp.NewReportStatus()
124			if err := report.Decode(respReader); err != nil {
125				return fmt.Errorf("decode report-status: %w", err)
126			}
127			if err := report.Error(); err != nil {
128				return err
129			}
130		}
131		return nil
132	}
133	
134	// PushObjects pushes locally-materialized objects to the target.
135	func PushObjects(
136		ctx context.Context,
137		conn *Conn,
138		adv *packp.AdvRefs,
139		commands []PushCommand,
140		store storer.Storer,
141		hashes []plumbing.Hash,
142		verbose bool,
143	) error {
144		req, _, hasUpdates, err := buildUpdateRequest(adv, commands, verbose)
145		if err != nil {
146			return err
147		}
148		if !hasUpdates {
149			return sendReceivePack(ctx, conn, req, nil)
150		}
151	
152		useRefDeltas := !adv.Capabilities.Supports(capability.OFSDelta)
153		pr, pw := io.Pipe()
154		done := make(chan error, 1)
155	
156		go func() {
157			enc := packfile.NewEncoder(pw, store, useRefDeltas)
158			if _, err := enc.Encode(hashes, 10); err != nil {
159				done <- pw.CloseWithError(fmt.Errorf("encode packfile: %w", err))
160				return
161			}
162			done <- pw.Close()
163		}()
164	
165		err = sendReceivePack(ctx, conn, req, pr)
166		_ = pr.Close()
167		encodeErr := <-done
168		if err != nil {
169			return err
170		}
171		return encodeErr
172	}
173	
174	// PushPack pushes a pack stream (relay) to the target.
175	func PushPack(
176		ctx context.Context,
177		conn *Conn,
178		adv *packp.AdvRefs,
179		commands []PushCommand,
180		pack io.ReadCloser,
181		verbose bool,
182	) error {
183		for _, cmd := range commands {
184			if cmd.Delete {
185				_ = pack.Close()
186				return fmt.Errorf("pack push only supports create and update actions")
187			}
188		}
189	
190		req, _, _, err := buildUpdateRequest(adv, commands, verbose)
191		if err != nil {
192			_ = pack.Close()
193			return err
194		}
195	
196		err = sendReceivePack(ctx, conn, req, pack)
197		closeErr := pack.Close()
198		if err != nil {
199			return err
200		}
201		return closeErr
202	}
203	
204	// PushCommands sends ref update commands without a pack (for ref-only changes).
205	func PushCommands(
206		ctx context.Context,
207		conn *Conn,
208		adv *packp.AdvRefs,
209		commands []PushCommand,
210		verbose bool,
211	) error {
212		req, _, _, err := buildUpdateRequest(adv, commands, verbose)
213		if err != nil {
214			return err
215		}
216		return sendReceivePack(ctx, conn, req, nil)
217	}
218

220		if !verbose {
221			return nil
222		}

When verbose is false it returns nil so the\n// demuxer discards progress frames without allocating.\nfunc progressSink(verbose bool, prefix string) io.Writer {\n\tif !verbose {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\treturn &prefixedLineWriter{w: os.Stderr, prefix: prefix}\n}\n\n// prefixedLineWriter writes each line of input prefixed with a fixed string.\n// Git sideband progress often arrives as chunks that contain embedded '\\r'\n// (carriage returns used to rewrite the current line, e.g. \"Resolving\n// deltas:  12%\\r\"). We treat both '\\n' and '\\r' as line terminators so\n// progress updates remain visible without double-printing.\ntype prefixedLineWriter struct {\n\tw       io.Writer\n\tprefix  string\n\tneedPfx bool\n}\n\nfunc (p *prefixedLineWriter) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {\n\tif len(b) == 0 {\n\t\treturn 0, nil\n\t}\n\twritten := 0\n\tstart := 0\n\t// Emit prefix lazily: only when we're about to write the first byte of\n\t// a new line. We treat both '\\n' and '\\r' as line terminators so\n// progress updates remain visible without double-printing.\ntype prefixedLineWriter struct {\n\tw       io.Writer\n\tprefix  string\n\tneedPfx bool\n}\n\nfunc (p *prefixedLineWriter) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {\n\tif len(b) == 0 {\n\t\treturn 0, nil\n\t}\n\twritten := 0\n\tstart := 0\n\t// Emit prefix lazily: only when we're about to write the first byte of\n\t// a new line. This avoids a trailing bare \"target: \" at EOF.\n\tif !p.needPfx {\n\t\tif _, err := io.WriteString(p.w, p.prefix); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn 0, err\n\t\t}\n\t\tp.needPfx = true\n\t}\n\tfor i, c := range b {\n\t\tif c != '\\n' && c != '\\r' {\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tn, err := p.w.Write(b[start : i+1])\n\t\twritten += n\n\t\tif err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn written, err\n\t\t}\n\t\tstart = i + 1\n\t\tif start < len(b) {\n\t\t\tif _, err := io.WriteString(p.w, p.prefix); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\treturn written, err\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t} else {\n\t\t\tp.needPfx = false\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tif start < len(b) {\n\t\tn, err := p.w.Write(b[start:])\n\t\twritten += n\n\t\tif err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn written, err\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn written, nil\n}",
  "new_string": "// progressSink returns a line-prefixing io.Writer suitable for\n// sideband.Demuxer.Progress. When verbose is false it returns nil so the\n// demuxer discards progress frames without allocating.\nfunc progressSink(verbose bool, prefix string) io.Writer {\n\tif !verbose {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\treturn &prefixedLineWriter{w: os.Stderr, prefix: prefix, atLineStart: true}\n}\n\n// prefixedLineWriter prepends a fixed prefix to each line of input written\n// to the wrapped writer. Git sideband progress arrives as chunks that may\n// contain '\\n' between full lines or '\\r' for in-place updates (\"Resolving\n// deltas:  12%\\r\"); both are treated as line terminators so the next chunk\n// gets a fresh prefix.\ntype prefixedLineWriter struct {\n\tw           io.Writer\n\tprefix      string\n\tatLineStart bool\n}\n\nfunc (p *prefixedLineWriter) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {\n\tconsumed := 0\n\tfor len(b) > 0 {\n\t\tif p.atLineStart {\n\t\t\tif _, err := io.WriteString(p.w, p.prefix); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\treturn consumed, err\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tp.atLineStart = false\n\t\t}\n\t\ti := bytes.IndexAny(b, \"\\r\\n\")\n\t\tvar chunk []byte\n\t\tif i < 0 {\n\t\t\tchunk = b\n\t\t} else {\n\t\t\tchunk = b[:i+1]\n\t\t\tp.atLineStart = true\n\t\t}\n\t\tn, err := p.w.Write(chunk)\n\t\tconsumed += n\n\t\tif err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn consumed, err\n\t\t}\n\t\tb = b[len(chunk):]\n\t}\n\treturn consumed, nil\n}"
}

29		switch protocolMode {
30		case "v1":
31			adv, refs, err := listSourceRefsV1(ctx, conn)
32			if err != nil {
33				return nil, nil, err
34			}
35			return refs, &RefService{Protocol: "v1", V1Adv: adv}, nil
36	
37		case "auto", "v2":
38			data, err := RequestInfoRefs(ctx, conn, transport.UploadPackService, "version=2")
39			if err != nil {

41			}

43				if !caps.Supports("ls-refs") || !caps.Supports("fetch") {
44					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("source does not advertise required protocol v2 commands")
45				}

47				if err != nil {
48					return nil, nil, err
49				}

51			}

53				return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("source did not negotiate protocol v2")
54			}

56			adv, err := decodeV1AdvRefs(data)

58				return nil, nil, err
59			}

188			return nil, git.NoErrAlreadyUpToDate
189		}

198		if hasTag(desired) && caps.FetchSupports("include-tag") {

214		if err != nil {

217		packStream, err := openV2PackStream(reader)

225	func storeV2FetchPack(store storer.Storer, r io.Reader) error {
226		reader := NewPacketReader(r)
227		for {
228			kind, payload, err := reader.ReadPacket()
229			if err != nil {
230				if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
231					return nil
232				}
233				return fmt.Errorf("decode protocol v2 fetch response: %w", err)
234			}
235			switch kind {
236			case PacketFlush:
237				return nil
238			case PacketDelim, PacketResponseEnd:
239				continue
240			case PacketData:
241				line := string(payload)
242				switch line {
243				case "packfile\n":
244					demux := sideband.NewDemuxer(sideband.Sideband64k, reader.BufReader())
245					return packfile.UpdateObjectStorage(store, demux)
246				case "acknowledgments\n", "shallow-info\n":
247					if err := SkipSection(reader); err != nil {
248						return err
249					}
250				default:
251					return fmt.Errorf("unexpected protocol v2 fetch section %q", strings.TrimSpace(line))
252				}
253			}
254		}
255	}
256	
257	func openV2PackStream(body io.ReadCloser) (io.ReadCloser, error) {
258		reader := NewPacketReader(body)
259		for {
260			kind, payload, err := reader.ReadPacket()
261			if err != nil {
262				if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
263					return nil, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF
264				}
265				return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode protocol v2 fetch response: %w", err)
266			}
267			switch kind {
268			case PacketFlush:
269				return nil, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF
270			case PacketDelim, PacketResponseEnd:
271				continue
272			case PacketData:
273				line := string(payload)
274				switch line {
275				case "packfile\n":
276					return &wrappedRC{
277						Reader: sideband.NewDemuxer(sideband.Sideband64k, reader.BufReader()),
278						Closer: body,
279					}, nil
280				case "acknowledgments\n", "shallow-info\n":
281					if err := SkipSection(reader); err != nil {
282						return nil, err
283					}
284				default:
285					return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected protocol v2 fetch section %q", strings.TrimSpace(line))
286				}
287			}
288		}
289	}

293	// buildV1UploadPackBody encodes a v1 upload-pack request body for stateless-rpc HTTP.
294	func buildV1UploadPackBody(
295		adv *packp.AdvRefs,
296		desired map[plumbing.ReferenceName]DesiredRef,
297		targetRefs map[plumbing.ReferenceName]plumbing.Hash,
298		includeTags bool,
299	) ([]byte, *capability.List, error) {
300		wants := collectWants(desired)
301		haves := SortedUniqueHashes(refValues(targetRefs))
302		if len(wants) == 0 {
303			return nil, nil, git.NoErrAlreadyUpToDate
304		}
305	
306		req := packp.NewUploadRequest()
307		req.Wants = wants
308		if adv.Capabilities.Supports(capability.NoProgress) {
309			_ = req.Capabilities.Set(capability.NoProgress)
310		}
311		if includeTags && adv.Capabilities.Supports(capability.IncludeTag) {
312			_ = req.Capabilities.Set(capability.IncludeTag)
313		}
314		// Prefer sideband64k over sideband (issue #4).
315		if sb := PreferredSideband(adv.Capabilities); sb != "" {
316			_ = req.Capabilities.Set(sb)
317		}
318		if adv.Capabilities.Supports(capability.OFSDelta) {

```
func buildSidebandReader(caps *capability.List, reader io.Reader, progress sideband.Progress) io.Reader {
	sb := PreferredSideband(caps)
	if sb == "" {
		return reader
	}
	var t sideband.Type
	if sb == capability.Sideband64k {
		t = sideband.Sideband64k
	} else {
		t = sideband.Sideband
	}
	d := sideband.NewDemuxer(t, reader)
	d.Progress = progress
	return d
}

Added a prefixedLineWriter that splits on both '\\n' and\n  '\\r' so in-place git progress updates (\"Resolving deltas: 12%\\r\")\n  remain readable when prefixed. progressSink returns nil for\n  non-verbose so the demuxer allocates nothing on the hot path.\n- fetch.go / refs.go: RefService gains a Verbose field. > AGENT

That's healthy progress — you're past the slow part. Here's what those logs are actually showing:

## What phase you're in

**21:18:11 → 21:22:02 (4 min): planning**
The `bootstrap batch fetching commit graph` line kicked off the probe phase. Each `source: Enumerating / Counting / Compressing / Total` block is a *separate* upload-pack round-trip to GitHub asking for tree:0 filtered packs along the master history. 13+ of those just to plan checkpoints.

The planning ended with:
```
bootstrap batch planned checkpoint branch=refs/heads/master checkpoint=a13ff0bb selected=1 chain_len=75767
```

Translation: master has a **75,767-commit** chain. Bootstrap picked **one** intermediate checkpoint. So the actual push will split into ~2 receive-pack POSTs for master plus one for tags — not 75k separate pushes, which is good.

**21:22:02 → now: fetching batch 1**
```
source: Enumerating objects: 2011027, done.
source: Counting objects: 100% (204362/204362), done.
source: Compressing objects: 100% (41832/41832), done.
```

That's **~2 million objects** being packaged on GitHub's side for the first batch (up to the `a13ff0bb` checkpoint). You should next see GitHub emit a "Writing objects: X%" progress line as it streams the pack to us — that's the multi-GB download. Then once it arrives, your client relays it to entire's receive-pack, and you'll see the `target:` lines start ("Unpacking objects: X%" / "Resolving deltas: X%").

## What to watch for next

- `source: Writing objects:` progress — pack being streamed from GitHub
- Stall or abrupt silence here = source-side rate-limit or TLS reset
- `target: Unpacking / Resolving deltas: X%` progress — entire-server processing the batch
- Stall here = entire chewing through delta resolution (watch CPU / heap in entire.log)
- A clean `bootstrap batch checkpoint complete ...` log = batch 1 landed, second batch starts
- A final `bootstrap batch branch finalized branch=refs/heads/master` = master is fully on target
- Then tag batches, then done

## Rough time estimate

GitHub has pack-reused a ton ("pack-reused 685000+" per probe fetch) so the actual pack is mostly pre-built. Network is the main bottleneck on the source side. For ~5 GB over a reasonable connection: 10–30 minutes to pull + push + process per batch.

Let it run. If it hangs for more than a few minutes without either side advancing, that's the real failure signal and we'll have a specific phase to debug.

> AGENT

Yes, they can be. Checkpoint selection is driven by `--batch-max-pack-bytes` using this heuristic (`internal/strategy/bootstrap/bootstrap.go:582`):

```
initialSpanCommits = batchMaxPack / 4096   // ~4 KiB per commit
```

At your current **256 MiB**, initial span ≈ **65,536 commits**. Your chain is 75,767 commits, so bootstrap selected 1 checkpoint at ~65k and pushes the remaining ~10k as a second batch. That also explains why you saw **13+ probe fetches** (the "bootstrap batch fetching commit graph" blocks): each one is a binary-search step narrowing down *where* to place that checkpoint.

## What bigger means in practice

| `--batch-max-pack-bytes` | initial span | likely checkpoints for linux | probe fetches | push payloads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256 MiB (now) | ~65k commits | 1 | many | ~2 × 2-3 GiB |
| 512 MiB | ~131k commits | **0** | few | 1 × ~5 GiB |
| 1 GiB | ~262k commits | 0 | 1-2 | 1 × ~5 GiB |
| 2 GiB | ~524k commits | 0 | 1 | 1 × ~5 GiB |
| unset | unbatched | 0 | 0 | 1 × ~5 GiB |

512 MiB or above likely collapses to a single master push with no checkpoint subdivision, which should cut ~3 minutes out of the planning phase.

## What to try

For a clean retry against an empty target:

```bash
time go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate -v \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --batch-max-pack-bytes 1073741824 \
  --max-pack-bytes 21474836480 \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT 2>&1 | tee /tmp/linux-replicate-1g.log
```

Bonus: bootstrap has an **auto-shrink** safety net (`autoBatchMaxPackBytes` in `bootstrap.go:132`). If the first push gets rejected for size, it will retry with smaller batches automatically. So starting big is low-risk.

## The real question: can entire's receive-pack handle a single ~5 GiB push?

That's the unknown. With `--batch-max-pack-bytes 268435456` the ongoing run will tell us if even 256 MiB batches push OK. If that works, try 1 GiB next time. If 256 MiB batches *don't* survive, bigger won't help either and we'll need to look at entire's limits (connect-go message size, raft WAL ingestion, etc.).

Easiest data point for right now: **let the current run finish or fail**. If it finishes, you know 256 MiB works end-to-end and you can try bigger on the next empty-target run.

what does pack-reused mean exactly where does this come from?

> AGENT

Those are git-core's own `pack-objects` counters, rendered on sideband channel 2 during upload-pack. They're not go-git — they come from GitHub's git binary. Format:

```
Total N (delta D), reused R (delta Dr), pack-reused P (from C)
```

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Total N** | total objects being placed in the response pack |
| **delta D** | how many of those are stored as delta objects (vs. whole/base objects) |
| **reused R** | objects found in an existing packfile that the server could emit without recompressing; still had to inspect/rewrite their headers |
| **delta Dr** | how many of those `reused` were delta-encoded (almost always equals `reused` — servers prefer not to materialize deltas) |
| **pack-reused P** | objects copied **byte-for-byte** from an existing packfile's data stream, zero inspection, zero recompression |
| **from C** | how many source packfiles the `pack-reused` bytes came from |

## Why it matters for your run

Look at one of your lines:

```
Total 702386 (delta 15429), reused 14062 (delta 14062), pack-reused 685362 (from 1)
```

- 702,386 total objects in the pack being sent
- 14,062 objects (2%) needed the "inspect-and-emit" path
- **685,362 objects (97.6%) were copied raw** from one pre-built pack
- so GitHub essentially hit a precomputed reachability slice and streamed those bytes verbatim

That's the optimization tier:

```
fastest: pack-reused   ← zero-cost byte copy
medium:  reused        ← existing object, write fresh header
slowest: fresh encode  ← enumerate, delta, compress from scratch
```

## Where the code is

In git-core it's `builtin/pack-objects.c`. The summary line is written by `write_pack_file` → the `progress` variable at end-of-pack. Search for `pack-reused` in that file if you ever want to read the producer.

go-git also has its own implementation in `plumbing/transport/upload_pack.go` — grep for `reused`:

> AGENT

Right — **go-git doesn't implement pack-reuse at all**. Its upload-pack always enumerates and re-encodes from scratch. Another reason GitHub serves big repos in seconds while a go-git-based source would take much longer for the same closure.

## Takeaway for your replicate run

The high `pack-reused` ratio is why your 13 probe fetches each finished quickly despite moving 500k+ objects per probe — GitHub wasn't really "counting" anything, it was just streaming a prebuilt pack-slice byte-for-byte. The planning time was dominated by network, not server CPU. So on the source side your throughput ceiling is just your pipe to GitHub.

The receiving side is where it can get expensive: **entire's receive-pack has to decompress, verify, resolve, and commit every one of those objects to its raft-backed storage**, so the `target: Unpacking / Resolving deltas` progress you'll see next is doing real work, not a byte copy. That's where batch sizing matters.

> AGENT

This is a good investigation question. The answer is **moderate effort, not hard** — the core plumbing already supports different source and target refs. Here's exactly where it works today and where it doesn't.

## What already works

The `DesiredRef` model and all downstream strategy code (plans, relay, push) fully support `SourceRef ≠ TargetRef`. The `--map` flag proves this end-to-end:

```bash
# This already works — pushes source refs/heads/main to target refs/heads/stable
git-sync replicate --map refs/heads/main:refs/heads/stable $SRC $TGT
```

Push commands just send whatever `TargetRef` the plan says. Receive-pack accepts any valid ref under `refs/`.

## What blocks `refs/gh/` prefixing today

**1. No bulk prefix transform — only 1:1 mappings** (`internal/planner/planner.go:53-73`)

Without `--map`, `BuildDesiredRefs` identity-maps all refs (source = target). With `--map`, you get explicit pairs. There's no `--map-prefix refs/:refs/gh/` to transform all matched refs in bulk.

**2. Tags always identity-map** (`planner.go:76-85`)

```go
// Tags bypass --map entirely
if err := addManaged(refName, refName, RefKindTag, hash); err != nil {
```

Even with mappings, tags always go to the same ref name. A prefix feature would need to intercept this.

**3. Validation rejects unknown ref kinds** (`internal/validation/validation.go:82-89`)

```go
if srcKind == "" {
    return ..., fmt.Errorf("unsupported source ref kind: %s", src)
}
```

`refKind()` only recognizes `refs/heads/` and `refs/tags/`. A ref like `refs/gh/heads/main` returns `""` → rejected.

**4. Relay eligibility checks branch/tag patterns** (`internal/planner/relay.go:126-138`)

```go
case RefKindBranch:
    if !plan.SourceRef.IsBranch() || !plan.TargetRef.IsBranch() {
        return false, "replicate-non-branch-mapping"
    }
```

`IsBranch()` is `strings.HasPrefix(ref, "refs/heads/")`. A `refs/gh/heads/main` target fails this.

## What you'd need to change

| Change | Effort | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Add `--target-prefix refs/gh/` flag (CLI + types) | easy | none |
| Apply prefix in `BuildDesiredRefs` before `addManaged` for both branches and tags | easy | low |
| Relax `refKind` / `NormalizeMapping` to accept custom namespaces or introduce `RefKindCustom` | medium | need to audit all callers |
| Relax relay eligibility to use a ref's *logical* kind (branch/tag based on source) rather than checking target ref prefix | medium | must verify receive-pack handles non-standard refs correctly |
| Prune logic: decide what "managed" means in the prefixed namespace | design decision | depends on semantics |

Nothing in the git protocol or receive-pack cares about ref naming — any ref under `refs/` works. So it's purely planner/validation/relay changes.

## Rough implementation sketch

```go
// In BuildDesiredRefs, after determining targetRef:
if cfg.TargetPrefix != "" {
    // refs/heads/main → refs/gh/heads/main
    targetRef = plumbing.ReferenceName(cfg.TargetPrefix + strings.TrimPrefix(string(sourceRef), "refs/"))
}
```

And carry the source-side `RefKind` through to the plan instead of re-deriving it from the target ref name. That single conceptual change (kind comes from source, not target pattern) unlocks arbitrary target namespaces.

## Design questions to settle first

- **Keep original branches on target too, or only prefixed?** If only prefixed, `refs/heads/main` doesn't exist on target — only `refs/gh/heads/main`. If both, you need two plans per ref.
- **Prune semantics**: does `--prune` delete `refs/gh/heads/stale` when source drops `refs/heads/stale`? Probably yes, but only within the prefixed namespace.
- **Tags**: prefix them too (`refs/gh/tags/v1.0`) or keep them at `refs/tags/v1.0`? Or configurable?
- **Multiple sources**: if you later want `refs/gh/` *and* `refs/gl/` (GitHub + GitLab), the prefix becomes per-source. That's a design fork worth thinking about now even if you only implement one source initially.

Overall: **~1 day of focused work**, mostly in planner + validation. No protocol changes, no strategy rewrites. The hardest part is the design decisions, not the code.

> AGENT

Two separate issues:

**1. Auth token expired mid-run.** The bootstrap planning took hours (all those probe fetches). By the time it started pushing, the `entiredb` OAuth token had expired. The refresh failed (or the refresh token itself expired), so the push got a 401.

Fix: re-login before retrying, and the token will be fresh for the push phase.

```bash
entiredb auth login
```

Then retry. With larger batches (1 GiB), planning is much faster, so the token is less likely to expire before the push.

**2. No `target:` lines.** That's because the push never got far enough to receive sideband progress — it was rejected at the HTTP level (401) before the receive-pack even started processing. If auth had succeeded, you'd see `target: Unpacking objects: ...` etc. during pack processing.

There's also a second reason: entire's receive-pack is go-git-based, and go-git's `transport.ReceivePack` doesn't emit progress messages on sideband channel 2 — the `TODO: support thin-pack` server also doesn't send progress updates during unpacking/resolving. So even with a successful push, you'd see `source:` lines but likely silence on the `target:` side until the report-status comes back. Real git-core servers (GitHub, GitLab, Gitea with git backend) would emit target progress.

**Recommended retry:**

```bash
entiredb auth login

time go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate -v \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --batch-max-pack-bytes 1073741824 \
  --max-pack-bytes 21474836480 \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT 2>&1 | tee /tmp/linux-replicate-2.log
```

The 1 GiB batch size should collapse planning from ~4 min / 13 probes to ~1 min / 1-2 probes, keeping the whole run well within the token's lifetime.

> AGENT

Your instinct is right — planning is doing way more work than it should for this case. Here's exactly what's happening and why it's wasteful:

## What the planning phase actually does

```
Step 1: fetch commit graph          → 1 fetch (tree:0 filter, commits only)
        Walk first-parent chain     → 75,767 commits for linux/master

Step 2: binary-search for where to place checkpoint boundaries
        For each probe candidate:
            → actual FetchPack from GitHub   ← THIS IS THE EXPENSIVE PART
            → download the FULL pack
            → measure its size
            → decide: fits under 256 MiB? yes → try wider. no → try narrower.
```

**Every single one of those `source: Enumerating objects: 700000` blocks was a real pack download.** The planner downloaded ~500K-700K objects (~200-300 MiB) per probe, **13+ times**, just to measure where the 256 MiB boundary falls. That's ~3-4 GiB of throwaway data downloaded during planning alone.

The 1 probe result that actually fit gets saved (`prefetched`) and reused for the push. The other 12+ are discarded.

## Why it's designed this way

The comment in `initialCheckpointSpan` explains the thinking:

```go
// Typical compressed commit + tree overhead averages ~2-5 KiB per commit
const avgBytesPerCommit = 4096
```

It starts with a commit-count heuristic (batch limit / 4 KiB), then **refines by measurement** because pack sizes are hard to predict (delta compression, GitHub's pack-reuse, blob sizes vary wildly). The binary search with real fetches is the refinement.

## Why it's wasteful for your case

At 256 MiB limit: `initialSpan = 268435456 / 4096 = 65,536 commits`. Chain = 75,767. So it starts with a guess that's close but doesn't cover the whole chain → binary search kicks in → many probes.

At 1 GiB limit: `initialSpan = 1073741824 / 4096 = 262,144 commits`. That's > 75,767 → the planner tries the whole chain as one batch on the first probe. If it fits (it will — linux master is ~4-5 GiB), done in 1-2 probes.

## The real answer to "can we not just guess?"

**Yes.** There are three progressively simpler approaches:

**A. Just try it and retry on failure (already half-implemented).**
`autoBatchMaxPackBytes` at `bootstrap.go:126` already retries with batching when a push gets rejected. So the optimal strategy for unknown targets is: push the whole thing. If it fails with a body-size error, split and retry. Zero planning probes. The retry path exists but is only triggered on *push rejection*, not used as the primary strategy.

**B. Estimate from commit count, never probe.**
Replace the binary search with pure arithmetic: `numBatches = ceil(chainLen * avgBytesPerCommit / batchLimit)`. Place checkpoints evenly. If a batch turns out too big, the target rejects it and you retry that batch at half size. No probe fetches ever.

**C. Just use large batches.**
Your immediate fix: `--batch-max-pack-bytes 2147483648` (2 GiB) or even omit it entirely and rely on auto-retry. Planning collapses to 1-2 fetches.

## What I'd recommend

For the near term: use a large batch limit (1-2 GiB) and let auto-retry handle target rejections. That's zero code changes and turns your 4-minute planning phase into ~30 seconds.

Longer term: option B (estimate-then-retry) is the right architecture. The probe-and-measure approach was built for precision but the precision isn't worth 13 round-trips to GitHub. A commit-count estimate with a 2x safety margin and a retry-on-rejection fallback would handle linux-sized repos in a fraction of the time. Want me to sketch that out?

78	// Execute runs the bootstrap strategy (one-shot or batched).
79	func Execute(ctx context.Context, p Params, relayReason string) (Result, error) {
80		if p.TargetPusher == nil {
81			return Result{Relay: true, RelayMode: "bootstrap", RelayReason: relayReason}, fmt.Errorf("bootstrap strategy requires TargetPusher")
82		}
83	
84		// GitHub large-repo preflight
85		if batchLimit, ok := githubBatchLimit(ctx, p); ok {
86			p.BatchMaxPack = batchLimit
87			p.log("bootstrap github preflight selected batched mode",
88				"batch_max_pack_bytes", p.BatchMaxPack)
89		}
90	
91		planTargetRefs := p.TargetRefs
92		if p.BatchMaxPack > 0 {
93			planTargetRefs = adjustedBootstrapTargetRefs(p.DesiredRefs, p.TargetRefs)
94		}
95		plans, err := planner.BuildBootstrapPlans(p.DesiredRefs, planTargetRefs)
96		if err != nil {
97			return Result{}, err
98		}
99	
100		result := Result{
101			Plans: plans, Relay: true, RelayMode: "bootstrap", RelayReason: relayReason,
102		}
103	
104		if p.BatchMaxPack > 0 {
105			return executeBatched(ctx, p, plans, result)
106		}
107	
108		// One-shot bootstrap
109		p.log("bootstrap fetching refs from source", "ref_count", len(plans))
110		gpDesired := convert.DesiredRefs(p.DesiredRefs)
111		packReader, err := p.SourceService.FetchPack(ctx, p.SourceConn, gpDesired, nil)
112		if err != nil {
113			if errors.Is(err, git.NoErrAlreadyUpToDate) {
114				return result, nil
115			}
116			return result, fmt.Errorf("fetch source pack: %w", err)
117		}
118		packReader = gitproto.LimitPackReader(packReader, p.MaxPackBytes)
119		packReader = closeOnce(packReader)
120	
121		p.log("bootstrap pushing refs to target", "ref_count", len(plans))
122		cmds := convert.PlansToPushCommands(plans)
123		pushErr := p.TargetPusher.PushPack(ctx, cmds, packReader)
124		_ = packReader.Close()
125		if pushErr != nil {
126			autoBatch, ok := autoBatchMaxPackBytes(p, pushErr)
127			if !ok {
128				return result, fmt.Errorf("push target refs: %w", pushErr)
129			}
130			p.log("bootstrap retrying with batched mode after target rejection",
131				"batch_max_pack_bytes", autoBatch)
132			p.BatchMaxPack = autoBatch
133			return executeBatched(ctx, p, plans, result)
134		}
135	
136		result.Pushed = len(plans)
137		return result, nil
138	}

163		ctx context.Context,
164		p Params,

168		if !p.SourceService.SupportsBootstrapBatch() {

320	func planBatches(ctx context.Context, p Params, desired []planner.DesiredRef) ([]plannedBatch, error) {
321		out := make([]plannedBatch, 0, len(desired))
322		for _, ref := range desired {
323			checkpoints, prefetched, err := planCheckpointsWithCache(ctx, p, ref)
324			if err != nil {
325				return nil, err
326			}
327			out = append(out, plannedBatch{
328				BootstrapBatch: planner.BootstrapBatch{
329					Plan: planner.BranchPlan{
330						Branch: ref.Label, SourceRef: ref.SourceRef,
331						TargetRef: ref.TargetRef, SourceHash: ref.SourceHash,
332						Kind: ref.Kind, Action: planner.ActionCreate,
333					},
334					TempRef:     planner.BootstrapTempRef(ref.TargetRef),
335					ResumeHash:  p.TargetRefs[planner.BootstrapTempRef(ref.TargetRef)],
336					Checkpoints: checkpoints,
337				},
338				prefetchedPacks: prefetched,
339			})
340		}
341		return out, nil
342	}

20	// FirstParentChain walks the first-parent chain from tip back to root,
21	// returning the chain in root-to-tip order.
22	func FirstParentChain(store storer.EncodedObjectStorer, tip plumbing.Hash) ([]plumbing.Hash, error) {
23		commit, err := object.GetCommit(store, tip)
24		if err != nil {
25			return nil, err
26		}
27		chain := make([]plumbing.Hash, 0, 128)
28		for {
29			chain = append(chain, commit.Hash)
30			if len(commit.ParentHashes) == 0 {
31				break
32			}
33			commit, err = object.GetCommit(store, commit.ParentHashes[0])
34			if err != nil {

36			}
37		}
38		// Reverse in-place to get root-to-tip order.
39		for i, j := 0, len(chain)-1; i < j; i, j = i+1, j-1 {
40			chain[i], chain[j] = chain[j], chain[i]
41		}
42		return chain, nil
43	}

45	// SampledCheckpointCandidates generates a set of candidate indices to probe,
46	// sorted from largest (preferred) to smallest.
47	func SampledCheckpointCandidates(lo, hi int, prevSpan int) []int {
48		if lo > hi {
49			return nil
50		}
51		set := map[int]struct{}{}
52		add := func(idx int) {
53			if idx < lo {
54				idx = lo
55			}
56			if idx > hi {
57				idx = hi
58			}
59			set[idx] = struct{}{}
60		}
61	
62		projected := hi
63		if prevSpan > 0 {
64			projected = lo + prevSpan - 1
65		}
66		add(projected)
67	
68		const sampleCount = 4
69		current := projected
70		for i := 0; i < sampleCount-1; i++ {
71			if current <= lo {
72				add(lo)
73				continue
74			}
75			distance := current - lo
76			current = lo + distance/2
77			add(current)
78		}
79		add(lo)
80	
81		candidates := make([]int, 0, len(set))
82		for idx := range set {
83			candidates = append(candidates, idx)
84		}
85		sort.Sort(sort.Reverse(sort.IntSlice(candidates)))
86		return candidates
87	}

89	// SampledCheckpointUnderLimit finds the largest checkpoint index that fits within
90	// the batch limit, using a sampling strategy to reduce probes (issue #14).
91	func SampledCheckpointUnderLimit(
92		chain []plumbing.Hash,
93		prevIdx int,
94		prevSpan int,
95		probe func(idx int) (tooLarge bool, err error),
96	) (int, error) {
97		lo := prevIdx + 1
98		hi := len(chain) - 1
99		if lo > hi {
100			return -1, nil
101		}
102	
103		samples := SampledCheckpointCandidates(lo, hi, prevSpan)
104		best := -1
105		for _, idx := range samples {
106			tooLarge, err := probe(idx)
107			if err != nil {
108				return -1, err
109			}
110			if tooLarge {
111				continue
112			}
113			best = idx
114			break
115		}
116		if best != -1 {
117			return best, nil
118		}
119	
120		if prevSpan > 1 {
121			shrunk := prevSpan / 2
122			if shrunk < 1 {
123				shrunk = 1
124			}
125			idx := lo + shrunk - 1
126			if idx > hi {
127				idx = hi
128			}
129			if idx >= lo {
130				tooLarge, err := probe(idx)
131				if err != nil {
132					return -1, err
133				}
134				if !tooLarge {
135					return idx, nil
136				}
137			}
138		}
139	
140		tooLarge, err := probe(lo)
141		if err != nil {
142			return -1, err
143		}
144		if tooLarge {
145			return -1, nil
146		}
147		return lo, nil
148	}

150	// BootstrapResumeIndex finds the starting index in a checkpoint list given a resume hash.
151	func BootstrapResumeIndex(checkpoints []plumbing.Hash, resumeHash plumbing.Hash) (int, error) {
152		if resumeHash.IsZero() {
153			return 0, nil
154		}
155		for idx, checkpoint := range checkpoints {
156			if checkpoint == resumeHash {
157				return idx + 1, nil
158			}
159		}
160		return 0, fmt.Errorf("temp ref hash %s does not match any planned checkpoint", resumeHash)
161	}

String: // --- Checkpoint planning ---

func planBatches(ctx context.Context, p Params, desired []planner.DesiredRef) ([]plannedBatch, error) {
	out := make([]plannedBatch, 0, len(desired))
	for _, ref := range desired {
		checkpoints, prefetched, err := planCheckpointsWithCache(ctx, p, ref)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		out = append(out, plannedBatch{
			BootstrapBatch: planner.BootstrapBatch{
				Plan: planner.BranchPlan{
					Branch: ref.Label, SourceRef: ref.SourceRef,
					TargetRef: ref.TargetRef, SourceHash: ref.SourceHash,
					Kind: ref.Kind, Action: planner.ActionCreate,
				},
				TempRef:     planner.BootstrapTempRef(ref.TargetRef),
				ResumeHash:  p.TargetRefs[planner.BootstrapTempRef(ref.TargetRef)],
				Checkpoints: checkpoints,
			},
			prefetchedPacks: prefetched,
		})
	}
	return out, nil
}

// PlanCheckpoints plans the checkpoint hashes for a single branch during batched bootstrap.
func PlanCheckpoints(ctx context.Context, p Params, ref planner.DesiredRef) ([]plumbing.Hash, error) {
	checkpoints, _, err := planCheckpointsWithCache(ctx, p, ref)
	return checkpoints, err
}

func planCheckpointsWithCache(ctx context.Context, p Params, ref planner.DesiredRef) ([]plumbing.Hash, map[plumbing.Hash][]byte, error) {
	cp, err := newCheckpointPlanner(ctx, p, ref)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, err
	}
	return cp.plan()
}

type probeResult struct {
	tooLarge bool
	data     []byte
}

type checkpointPlanner struct {
	ctx        context.Context
	params     Params
	ref        planner.DesiredRef
	chain      []plumbing.Hash
	probeCache map[string]probeResult
	prefetched map[plumbing.Hash][]byte
}

func newCheckpointPlanner(ctx context.Context, p Params, ref planner.DesiredRef) (*checkpointPlanner, error) {
	p.log("bootstrap batch fetching commit graph", "branch", ref.TargetRef.String())
	graphStore := memory.NewStorage()
	gpRef := gitproto.DesiredRef{SourceRef: ref.SourceRef, TargetRef: ref.TargetRef, SourceHash: ref.SourceHash}
	if err := p.SourceService.FetchCommitGraph(ctx, graphStore, p.SourceConn, gpRef); err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("fetch bootstrap planning graph for %s: %w", ref.TargetRef, err)
	}
	chain, err := planner.FirstParentChain(graphStore, ref.SourceHash)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("walk first-parent chain for %s: %w", ref.TargetRef, err)
	}
	if len(chain) == 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("empty first-parent chain for %s", ref.TargetRef)
	}
	return &checkpointPlanner{
		ctx:        ctx,
		params:     p,
		ref:        ref,
		chain:      chain,
		probeCache: make(map[string]probeResult),
		prefetched: make(map[plumbing.Hash][]byte),
	}, nil
}

func (p *checkpointPlanner) plan() ([]plumbing.Hash, map[plumbing.Hash][]byte, error) {
	checkpoints := make([]plumbing.Hash, 0, len(p.chain))
	prevIdx := -1
	prevHash := plumbing.ZeroHash
	prevSpan := initialCheckpointSpan(p.params.BatchMaxPack, len(p.chain))
	prevMeasuredBytes := 0
	for prevIdx < len(p.chain)-1 {
		bestIdx, err := p.selectNextCheckpoint(prevIdx, prevHash, prevSpan, prevMeasuredBytes)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, err
		}
		if bestIdx <= prevIdx {
			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("could not find bootstrap checkpoint for %s under batch-max-pack-bytes=%d", p.ref.TargetRef, p.params.BatchMaxPack)
		}
		if result, ok := p.cachedProbe(prevHash, bestIdx); ok && !result.tooLarge && len(result.data) > 0 {
			p.prefetched[p.chain[bestIdx]] = result.data
			prevSpan = adaptiveNextProbeSpan(p.params.BatchMaxPack, len(result.data), bestIdx-prevIdx, len(p.chain)-1-bestIdx)
			prevMeasuredBytes = len(result.data)
		} else {
			prevSpan = bestIdx - prevIdx
			prevMeasuredBytes = 0
		}
		prevIdx = bestIdx
		prevHash = p.chain[bestIdx]
		checkpoints = append(checkpoints, prevHash)
		p.params.log("bootstrap batch planned checkpoint",
			"branch", p.ref.TargetRef.String(),
			"checkpoint", planner.ShortHash(prevHash),
			"selected", len(checkpoints),
			"chain_len", len(p.chain))
	}
	return checkpoints, p.prefetched, nil
}

func (p *checkpointPlanner) selectNextCheckpoint(prevIdx int, prevHash plumbing.Hash, prevSpan int, prevMeasuredBytes int) (int, error) {
	bestIdx := -1
	remaining := len(p.chain) - 1 - prevIdx
	if shouldSelectTipWithoutProbe(p.params.BatchMaxPack, prevMeasuredBytes, prevSpan, remaining) {
		bestIdx = len(p.chain) - 1
	} else if shouldProbeTipFirst(p.params.BatchMaxPack, prevMeasuredBytes, prevSpan, remaining) {
		tipIdx := len(p.chain) - 1
		tooLarge, err := p.probe(prevHash, tipIdx)
		if err != nil {
			return -1, err
		}
		if !tooLarge {
			bestIdx = tipIdx
		}
	}
	if bestIdx != -1 {
		return bestIdx, nil
	}
	return p.searchCheckpointUnderLimit(prevIdx, prevHash, prevSpan)
}

func (p *checkpointPlanner) probe(prevHash plumbing.Hash, idx int) (bool, error) {
	if result, ok := p.cachedProbe(prevHash, idx); ok {
		return result.tooLarge, nil
	}
	data, tooLarge, err := fetchPackForProbe(p.ctx, p.params, p.ref, p.chain[idx], prevHash, p.params.BatchMaxPack)
	if err != nil {
		return false, fmt.Errorf("measure bootstrap batch for %s at %s: %w", p.ref.TargetRef, planner.ShortHash(p.chain[idx]), err)
	}
	p.probeCache[probeKey(prevHash, idx)] = probeResult{tooLarge: tooLarge, data: data}
	return tooLarge, nil
}

func (p *checkpointPlanner) cachedProbe(prevHash plumbing.Hash, idx int) (probeResult, bool) {
	result, ok := p.probeCache[probeKey(prevHash, idx)]
	return result, ok
}

func (p *checkpointPlanner) probeBounds(prevHash plumbing.Hash, lo, hi int) (largestFit int, smallestTooLarge int) {
	largestFit = lo - 1
	smallestTooLarge = hi + 1
	for idx := lo; idx <= hi; idx++ {
		result, ok := p.cachedProbe(prevHash, idx)
		if !ok {
			continue
		}
		if result.tooLarge {
			if idx < smallestTooLarge {
				smallestTooLarge = idx
			}
			continue
		}
		if idx > largestFit {
			largestFit = idx
		}
	}
	return largestFit, smallestTooLarge
}

func (p *checkpointPlanner) searchCheckpointUnderLimit(prevIdx int, prevHash plumbing.Hash, prevSpan int) (int, error) {
	lo := prevIdx + 1
	hi := len(p.chain) - 1
	if lo > hi {
		return -1, nil
	}

	largestFit, smallestTooLarge := p.probeBounds(prevHash, lo, hi)
	if smallestTooLarge > hi {
		if largestFit >= lo {
			return largestFit, nil
		}

		idx := nextCheckpointProbeCandidate(lo, hi, prevSpan, largestFit, smallestTooLarge)
		tooLarge, err := p.probe(prevHash, idx)
		if err != nil {
			return -1, err
		}
		if !tooLarge {
			return idx, nil
		}
		smallestTooLarge = idx
	}

	for smallestTooLarge-largestFit > 1 {
		idx := nextCheckpointProbeCandidate(lo, hi, prevSpan, largestFit, smallestTooLarge)
		if idx <= largestFit {
			idx = largestFit + 1
		}
		if idx >= smallestTooLarge {
			idx = smallestTooLarge - 1
		}
		if idx < lo || idx > hi || idx <= largestFit || idx >= smallestTooLarge {
			break
		}

		tooLarge, err := p.probe(prevHash, idx)
		if err != nil {
			return -1, err
		}
		if tooLarge {
			smallestTooLarge = idx
			continue
		}
		largestFit = idx
	}

	if largestFit >= lo {
		return largestFit, nil
	}

	tooLarge, err := p.probe(prevHash, lo)
	if err != nil {
		return -1, err
	}
	if tooLarge {
		return -1, nil
	}
	return lo, nil
}

func probeKey(prevHash plumbing.Hash, idx int) string {
	return prevHash.String() + ":" + strconv.Itoa(idx)
}

func initialCheckpointSpan(batchMaxPack int64, chainLen int) int {
	// Issue #14: Use a commit-count heuristic for the initial span estimate
	// to reduce expensive fetch-and-discard probes. Typical compressed commit
	// + tree overhead averages ~2-5 KiB per commit in a mature repo.
	const avgBytesPerCommit = 4096
	if batchMaxPack <= 0 {
		return 0
	}
	initialSpan := int(batchMaxPack / avgBytesPerCommit)
	if initialSpan > chainLen {
		initialSpan = chainLen
	}
	if initialSpan < 1 {
		initialSpan = 1
	}
	return initialSpan
}

func adaptiveNextProbeSpan(limit int64, measuredBytes int, selectedSpan int, remaining int) int {
	if selectedSpan < 1 {
		selectedSpan = 1
	}
	if remaining < 1 {
		return selectedSpan
	}
	if limit <= 0 || measuredBytes <= 0 {
		if selectedSpan > remaining {
			return remaining
		}
		return selectedSpan
	}
	estimated := int(float64(selectedSpan) * float64(limit) / float64(measuredBytes))
	if estimated < 1 {
		estimated = 1
	}
	if estimated > remaining {
		estimated = remaining
	}
	return estimated
}

func shouldProbeTipFirst(batchMaxPack int64, prevMeasuredBytes int, prevSpan int, remaining int) bool {
	if batchMaxPack <= 0 || remaining <= 0 {
		return false
	}
	if prevMeasuredBytes > 0 && prevSpan > 0 {
		estimated := int64(float64(prevMeasuredBytes) * float64(remaining) / float64(prevSpan))
		return estimated <= batchMaxPack
	}
	return false
}

func shouldSelectTipWithoutProbe(batchMaxPack int64, prevMeasuredBytes int, prevSpan int, remaining int) bool {
	if batchMaxPack <= 0 || remaining <= 0 {
		return false
	}
	if prevMeasuredBytes > 0 && prevSpan > 0 {
		estimated := int64(float64(prevMeasuredBytes) * float64(remaining) / float64(prevSpan))
		return estimated <= batchMaxPack/2
	}
	return false
}

func nextCheckpointProbeCandidate(lo, hi, prevSpan, largestFit, smallestTooLarge int) int {
	if largestFit >= lo && smallestTooLarge <= hi {
		return (largestFit + smallestTooLarge) / 2
	}
	if largestFit >= lo {
		return largestFit + prevSpan
	}
	projected := lo + prevSpan - 1
	if projected > hi {
		return hi
	}
	return projected
}

func fetchPackForProbe(ctx context.Context, p Params, ref planner.DesiredRef, want, have plumbing.Hash, limit int64) ([]byte, bool, error) {
	desired := singleGP(ref.SourceRef, ref.TargetRef, want)
	haves := planner.SingleHaveMap(have)
	packReader, err := p.SourceService.FetchPack(ctx, p.SourceConn, desired, haves)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}
	defer packReader.Close()
	data, err := io.ReadAll(gitproto.LimitPackReader(packReader, limit))
	if err == nil {
		return data, false, nil
	}
	if strings.Contains(err.Error(), "source pack exceeded max-pack-bytes limit") {
		return nil, true, nil
	}
	return nil, false, err
}</tool_use_error>

## What changed

**Before**: 13+ full `FetchPack` round-trips to GitHub (each downloading ~300 MiB of pack data, discarded after measuring) just to decide where to place checkpoint boundaries. ~4 minutes of planning for linux/master.

**After**: 1 commit-graph fetch (~20s) → count commits → `ceil(75767 × 8KiB / batchLimit)` → evenly-spaced checkpoints. Zero probe fetches.

> AGENT

Planning worked perfectly — 48 seconds total vs the old 4+ minutes. The failure is a different issue: `LimitPackReader` is capping each batch's source fetch to `BatchMaxPack` (1 GiB), but since our estimate said 1 batch, the single fetch needs to carry the full ~5 GiB pack.

The batch limit should control checkpoint *placement* (how many batches), not abort the source fetch mid-stream. The user's `--max-pack-bytes` (20 GiB) is the hard abort threshold.

> DEVELOPER

I think the target has a 2Gb limit

> AGENT

Then split into more batches. At 8 KiB/commit estimate for 75k commits, you need to lower the batch limit so the estimate produces enough batches to keep real pack size under 2 GiB each.

Real pack is ~5 GiB for 75k commits → ~66 KiB/commit actual. To get batches under 2 GiB:

```
75k commits × 66 KiB ≈ 5 GiB total
5 GiB / 2 GiB = 3 batches needed
```

But our estimate uses 8 KiB/commit, so we need to set the batch limit low enough that `ceil(75k × 8KiB / limit) ≥ 3`:

```
75k × 8KiB = 600 MiB estimated
600 MiB / 3 = 200 MiB per batch → yields 3 batches
```

Each batch covers ~25k commits → actual ~1.7 GiB → under the 2 GiB target limit.

```bash

  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \

  --max-pack-bytes 21474836480 \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT 2>&1 | tee /tmp/linux-replicate-5.log
```

That's 200 MiB batch limit → 3 estimated batches → ~1.7 GiB actual per batch → under 2 GiB.

If 1.7 GiB is still too close to the limit (compression varies), drop to 128 MiB → 5 batches → ~1 GiB each:

> AGENT

Progress! Batch 1 (307 MiB) and batch 2 (1.4 GiB) landed. Batch 3 hit the 2 GiB limit — the last third of the chain has more objects than the first two thirds combined (6.5M vs 4.9M objects). The commit graph isn't uniform.

Good news: **resume will pick up from batch 2**. The temp ref `refs/gitsync/bootstrap/heads/master` is sitting at `3eab887a`. Just rerun with a smaller batch limit so the remaining ~50k commits get split into more pieces:

```bash
time go run ./cmd/git-sync replicate -v \
  --target-insecure-skip-tls-verify \
  --batch-max-pack-bytes 104857600 \
  --max-pack-bytes 21474836480 \
  --measure-memory --stats --json \
  $SRC $TGT 2>&1 | tee /tmp/linux-replicate-6.log
```

100 MiB batch limit → the remaining chain will split into ~6 batches of ~1 GiB actual each. The first 2 batches (already pushed) get skipped via resume.

The underlying issue is that object density varies wildly along the commit chain — early history is sparse, recent history is dense. Evenly spacing by commit count doesn't produce even pack sizes. That's a known limitation of the estimate approach. A future improvement could weight checkpoints by commit density (merge commits, file-count-per-commit from the graph), but for now, smaller batch limits are the safe path.

138	func adjustedBootstrapTargetRefs(
139		desiredRefs map[plumbing.ReferenceName]planner.DesiredRef,
140		targetRefs map[plumbing.ReferenceName]plumbing.Hash,
141	) map[plumbing.ReferenceName]plumbing.Hash {
142		if len(targetRefs) == 0 {
143			return targetRefs
144		}
145		adjusted := planner.CopyRefHashMap(targetRefs)
146		for targetRef, desired := range desiredRefs {
147			if desired.Kind != planner.RefKindBranch {
148				continue
149			}
150			tempRef := planner.BootstrapTempRef(targetRef)
151			if adjusted[targetRef] == desired.SourceHash && adjusted[tempRef] == desired.SourceHash {
152				adjusted[targetRef] = plumbing.ZeroHash
153			}
154		}
155		return adjusted
156	}

497	func autoBatchMaxPackBytes(p Params, err error) (int64, bool) {
498		if p.BatchMaxPack > 0 || !isTargetBodyLimitError(err) {
499			return 0, false
500		}
501		if p.SourceService == nil || !p.SourceService.SupportsBootstrapBatch() {
502			return 0, false
503		}
504		limit := int64(defaultAutoBatchMaxPackBytes)
505		if targetLimit := targetBodyLimit(err); targetLimit > 0 {
506			derived := targetLimit / 2
507			if derived <= 0 {
508				derived = targetLimit
509			}
510			if derived < limit {
511				limit = derived
512			}
513		}
514		if p.MaxPackBytes > 0 && p.MaxPackBytes < limit {
515			limit = p.MaxPackBytes
516		}
517		if limit <= 0 {
518			return 0, false
519		}
520		return limit, true
521	}
522	
523	func isTargetBodyLimitError(err error) bool {
524		if err == nil {
525			return false
526		}
527		msg := strings.ToLower(err.Error())
528		return strings.Contains(msg, "body exceeded size limit") ||
529			(strings.Contains(msg, "request body") && strings.Contains(msg, "too large")) ||
530			(strings.Contains(msg, "payload") && strings.Contains(msg, "too large")) ||
531			strings.Contains(msg, "http 413")
532	}
533	
534	func targetBodyLimit(err error) int64 {
535		if err == nil {
536			return 0
537		}
538		matches := bodyLimitPattern.FindStringSubmatch(strings.ToLower(err.Error()))
539		if len(matches) != 2 {
540			return 0
541		}
542		limit, parseErr := strconv.ParseInt(matches[1], 10, 64)
543		if parseErr != nil {
544			return 0
545		}
546		return limit
547	}

  "old_string": "// evenCheckpoints places numBatches checkpoints evenly along the chain.\n// The last checkpoint is always the tip (chain[len-1]).\nfunc evenCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, numBatches int) []plumbing.Hash {",
  "new_string": "// subdivideCheckpoints splits each remaining checkpoint range in half using\n// the full commit chain. Called when a batch push is rejected for exceeding\n// the target's body-size limit. Returns the expanded checkpoint list; if no\n// split is possible (ranges are already 1 commit), returns the input unchanged.\nfunc subdivideCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, current plumbing.Hash, remaining []plumbing.Hash) []plumbing.Hash {\n\tchainIdx := make(map[plumbing.Hash]int, len(chain))\n\tfor i, h := range chain {\n\t\tchainIdx[h] = i\n\t}\n\tcurIdx, ok := chainIdx[current]\n\tif !ok && !current.IsZero() {\n\t\treturn remaining // can't find current in chain, give up\n\t}\n\tif current.IsZero() {\n\t\tcurIdx = -1\n\t}\n\n\texpanded := make([]plumbing.Hash, 0, len(remaining)*2)\n\tprev := curIdx\n\tfor _, cp := range remaining {\n\t\tcpIdx, ok := chainIdx[cp]\n\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\texpanded = append(expanded, cp)\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tgap := cpIdx - prev\n\t\tif gap > 1 {\n\t\t\t// Insert midpoint\n\t\t\tmidIdx := prev + gap/2\n\t\t\texpanded = append(expanded, chain[midIdx])\n\t\t}\n\t\texpanded = append(expanded, cp)\n\t\tprev = cpIdx\n\t}\n\treturn expanded\n}\n\n// evenCheckpoints places numBatches checkpoints evenly along the chain.\n// The last checkpoint is always the tip (chain[len-1]).\nfunc evenCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, numBatches int) []plumbing.Hash {"

{

  "new_string": "}\n\n// subdivideCheckpoints splits each remaining checkpoint range in half using\n// the full commit chain. Called when a batch push is rejected for exceeding\n// the target's body-size limit. Returns the expanded checkpoint list; if no\n// split is possible (ranges are already 1 commit), returns the input unchanged.\nfunc subdivideCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, current plumbing.Hash, remaining []plumbing.Hash) []plumbing.Hash {\n\tchainIdx := make(map[plumbing.Hash]int, len(chain))\n\tfor i, h := range chain {\n\t\tchainIdx[h] = i\n\t}\n\tcurIdx, ok := chainIdx[current]\n\tif !ok && !current.IsZero() {\n\t\treturn remaining\n\t}\n\tif current.IsZero() {\n\t\tcurIdx = -1\n\t}\n\n\texpanded := make([]plumbing.Hash, 0, len(remaining)*2)\n\tprev := curIdx\n\tfor _, cp := range remaining {\n\t\tcpIdx, ok := chainIdx[cp]\n\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\texpanded = append(expanded, cp)\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tgap := cpIdx - prev\n\t\tif gap > 1 {\n\t\t\tmidIdx := prev + gap/2\n\t\t\texpanded = append(expanded, chain[midIdx])\n\t\t}\n\t\texpanded = append(expanded, cp)\n\t\tprev = cpIdx\n\t}\n\treturn expanded\n}\n\nfunc evenCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, numBatches int) []plumbing.Hash {"
}

{
  "command": "git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\nAuto-subdivide batches on target body-size rejection\n\nWhen a batched bootstrap push is rejected by the target for exceeding\nits body-size limit, instead of failing immediately, subdivide the\nremaining checkpoints by inserting midpoints from the stored commit\nchain and retry. Each failing batch gets split in half, halving the\ncommit range (and roughly halving the pack size) per retry. This\nconverges to batches small enough for the target without requiring the\nuser to manually lower --batch-max-pack-bytes and re-run.\n\nThe commit chain is already in memory from the planning phase (~1.5 MiB\nfor linux's 75k commits). subdivideCheckpoints walks the remaining\ncheckpoint list, computes chain-index gaps, and inserts a midpoint for\neach gap > 1 commit. Adjacent commits (gap=1) cannot be split further;\nif even a single-commit batch is too large, the push fails as before.\n\nExample for the linux kernel at 200 MiB batch estimate:\n  - Estimate plans 3 batches (25k commits each)\n  - Batch 3 contains 6.5M objects (~2.3 GiB), target limit is 2 GiB\n  - Push rejected → subdivide inserts midpoint → 4 checkpoints\n  - Retry batch 3a (~12.5k commits, ~1.2 GiB) → succeeds\n  - Continue batch 3b (~12.5k commits, ~1.1 GiB) → succeeds\n  - No user intervention needed\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\"",
  "description": "Commit auto-subdivide"
}

> DEVELOPER

stupid question: could we figure out while transfering from source to target that the packfile gets to big and then meanigful cut it?

> AGENT

Not a stupid question at all — it's the ideal solution. Instead of guessing batch sizes upfront, you'd stream from source and cut when approaching the target's limit. No estimation, no retry, one pass.

**The hard part**: a git packfile isn't arbitrarily splittable. The pack is a stream of delta-compressed objects where later objects may reference earlier ones as bases. You can't cut at an arbitrary byte offset and have two valid packs — the second half would reference bases that only exist in the first half.

**But**: you CAN cut at a *commit boundary* in the checkpoint chain. The key insight is that the commit chain gives you safe split points. If you're streaming objects for commits A→Z and you've passed the commit-B boundary, you can stop the stream, push what you have as "A→B", then start a new fetch for "B→Z".

The challenge is knowing which objects belong to which commit boundary while the pack is streaming. The source packs objects in an order optimized for delta compression, not in commit order. So "objects for commit B" are interleaved with objects for commits C-Z in the pack.

**What WOULD work**: a counting proxy that tracks bytes streamed and, when approaching the limit, signals the push to complete with a reduced ref update (only advance to the last known-safe checkpoint), then starts a new fetch for the remainder. This is essentially "streaming batching" — you don't know the batch boundaries until you're mid-stream.

Sketch:

```
source fetch(want=tip, have=current)
  → tee through byte counter
  → when counter passes threshold:
      - close the pack stream (source sends remaining objects, we discard)
      - push what we have as current→midpoint
      - start new fetch(want=tip, have=midpoint)
```

The problem: we can't "close early and have a valid pack." The pack header declares the object count upfront. Truncating violates that. The target's receive-pack would reject a truncated pack.

**What could actually work in practice**:

Rather than cutting mid-stream, use the `Content-Length` from the source's HTTP response (if present) to decide *before* pushing whether this batch needs splitting. GitHub sends `Content-Length` on pack responses. Check it, and if it's over the target's limit, abort the fetch, subdivide, and re-fetch smaller ranges. This is one extra HEAD-like round-trip per oversized batch — way cheaper than the old probe approach, and no wasted transfer.

That'd be a one-line check right after `FetchPack` returns, before forwarding to `PushPack`. Want me to look into whether the HTTP response exposes content-length through the reader chain?

> AGENT

No `Content-Length` — GitHub streams via HTTP/2. But there's something better we can read in **12 bytes**: the PACK header.

Every git packfile starts with `PACK<version:4><object-count:4>`. We can peek at those 12 bytes after FetchPack returns, estimate size from the object count, and abort before downloading the full pack.

```
estimated_size = object_count × ~750 bytes/object (compressed average)
```

For linux batch 3: 6.5M objects × 750 ≈ 4.9 GiB → way over 2 GiB limit → subdivide immediately, zero wasted transfer.

{
  "replace_all": false,
  "file_path": "/Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/git-sync/internal/strategy/bootstrap/bootstrap.go",
  "old_string": "// subdivideCheckpoints splits each remaining checkpoint range in half using",
  "new_string": "// estimatedBytesPerObject is a conservative average for compressed git objects\n// in a packfile. Used with the PACK header's object count to estimate total\n// pack size before streaming the full pack. Real values range from ~200 bytes\n// (tiny commits in a sparse repo) to ~2 KiB (blob-heavy repos), with most\n// mature repos averaging 500–1000 bytes. 750 is a reasonable middle ground.\nconst estimatedBytesPerObject = 750\n\n// checkPackSizeAndSubdivide reads the 12-byte PACK header to get the object\n// count, estimates total pack size, and if it exceeds batchLimit, closes the\n// reader and calls subdivide(). Returns (nil, nil) when subdivided (caller\n// should continue to retry), or (prepended reader, nil) to proceed with push.\nfunc checkPackSizeAndSubdivide(\n\tr io.ReadCloser,\n\tbatchLimit int64,\n\tsubdivide func() bool,\n) (io.ReadCloser, error) {\n\tvar header [12]byte\n\tn, err := io.ReadFull(r, header[:])\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\t// Short pack or error — let the push handle it\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:n]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil\n\t}\n\tif string(header[:4]) != \"PACK\" {\n\t\t// Not a standard packfile — can't estimate, proceed\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil\n\t}\n\tobjectCount := int64(header[8])<<24 | int64(header[9])<<16 | int64(header[10])<<8 | int64(header[11])\n\testimated := objectCount * estimatedBytesPerObject\n\n\tif estimated > batchLimit && subdivide() {\n\t\t_ = r.Close()\n\t\treturn nil, nil\n\t}\n\n\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil\n}\n\ntype wrappedMultiRC struct {\n\tio.Reader\n\tio.Closer\n}\n\nfunc (w *wrappedMultiRC) Read(p []byte) (int, error) { return w.Reader.Read(p) }\n\n// subdivideCheckpoints splits each remaining checkpoint range in half using"
}

Expected flow:
```
batch 1: skipped (resume)
batch 2: skipped (resume)
batch 3: fetch → PACK header: 6.5M objects × 750 = 4.9 GiB > 200 MiB
  → "subdividing before push (pack header estimate)"
  → re-plan: insert midpoint → now 4 checkpoints
batch 3a: fetch → PACK header: ~3M objects → ~2.2 GiB > 200 MiB
  → subdivide again → 6 checkpoints
batch 3a-i: fetch → ~1.5M objects → ~1.1 GiB > 200 MiB
  → subdivide again ...
  (converges in ~4 splits to batches under 2 GiB)
```

The splits happen in seconds (12-byte reads). Only the final correctly-sized fetches actually transfer data.

> AGENT

Exactly right. Two layers:

1. **Estimate upfront** (commit-count heuristic): `ceil(75k × 8KiB / batchLimit)` → place checkpoints evenly. This avoids most oversized fetches by starting with a reasonable split. Zero cost — just arithmetic on the chain length we already have.

2. **PACK header precheck** (12-byte peek): catches the cases where the estimate was wrong. Costs the source a full `pack-objects` run (it builds the pack before we can see the header), but we abort after 12 bytes instead of streaming 5 GiB to the target and getting rejected.

So yes — the source still does the work of building the pack. That's unavoidable with git's protocol (there's no "how big would this pack be?" query). But we avoid:
- Downloading the full oversized pack (GiBs of wasted network)
- Pushing it to the target (GiBs of wasted upload)
- The target processing and then rejecting it (GiBs of wasted CPU/IO)

The wasted source-side pack-objects run is typically 10-30 seconds for a large batch — annoying but tolerable, and it only happens when the estimate was wrong (which gets rarer as the checkpoints get finer through subdivision).
